government.name: City of Langley
government.howBuilt: This list draws on City of Langley election and budget information, the platforms of the two elector organizations, official candidate profiles, and local news coverage of the 2026 campaign, including the 2026 budget, the end of the shared RCMP detachment with the Township, and the facility opinion vote. We kept issues the City of Langley can act on through zoning, its budget, bylaws, streets, parks, and services. Issues mainly run by the province, such as health care and mental health services, are left out of this list.

issues.title: Housing growth and density
issues.description: How much new housing Langley City allows, what kinds of buildings, and where they go as SkyTrain arrives.
issues.whatItAffects: Renters, buyers, families, seniors, and people living in single-family neighbourhoods.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets zoning and the Official Community Plan, approves rezonings and housing agreements, and sets development charges.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach new housing?
viewQuestion.poleA: Allow more apartments and mixed-use buildings in more parts of the city
viewQuestion.poleB: Keep larger buildings near SkyTrain and downtown, and protect single-family areas

tradeoffs.context: Housing decisions trade how fast and where new homes get built against how much existing neighbourhoods change.

gains: More homes, including rentals, could be built sooner across the city
More people near shops and transit may support local businesses
costs: Single-family streets may see more traffic, parking pressure, and change in character
Pipes, roads, and schools may need upgrades sooner

gains: Established neighbourhoods may keep their current scale and feel
Growth can be focused where SkyTrain and services already are
costs: Fewer new homes could keep rents and prices higher for longer
Fewer housing choices may be available outside the downtown and station areas

issues.title: Property taxes and city spending
issues.description: How much property taxes rise each year and what the city spends money on.
issues.whatItAffects: Homeowners, renters (through rent), businesses, and everyone who uses city services.
issues.whoDecides: Council adopts the annual budget and five-year financial plan, sets the tax rate, and decides staffing and project spending.

viewQuestion.question: What should guide the city budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep adding staff and services as the city grows, even if taxes rise
viewQuestion.poleB: Hold tax increases down, even if some services or projects wait

tradeoffs.context: Budgets are limited, so more spending on staff and services usually means higher taxes, and lower taxes usually mean doing less.

gains: More police, firefighters, and services could keep pace with growth
Projects and repairs may happen sooner
costs: Property tax bills may keep rising faster than inflation
Higher costs may pass through to renters and businesses

gains: Tax bills may grow more slowly for owners, renters, and businesses
Spending reviews may find savings in existing budgets
costs: Some new staff, services, or projects may be delayed or dropped
Deferred spending may cost more later

issues.title: Community safety
issues.description: How the city responds to crime, disorder, and safety concerns downtown and in parks, now that the shared RCMP detachment with the Township is ending.
issues.whatItAffects: Residents, business owners, visitors, and people living on the street.
issues.whoDecides: Council funds the City's RCMP contract, firefighters, bylaw and community safety officers, and decides how much goes to enforcement versus prevention programs.

viewQuestion.question: Where should the city put more of its safety budget?
viewQuestion.poleA: More police, bylaw, and community safety officers
viewQuestion.poleB: More prevention, outreach, and community-led programs

tradeoffs.context: Safety budgets are limited, so more spending on enforcement often means less for prevention, and the reverse.

gains: A visible patrol presence may help people feel safer downtown and in parks
Faster response to calls about crime and disorder
costs: Policing costs may raise taxes or take money from other services
Enforcement may move problems elsewhere rather than resolve them

gains: Programs may address some causes of disorder before they escalate
Residents and groups get a bigger role in shaping safety
costs: Results may take longer to show
Some residents may feel less safe without more officers on patrol

issues.title: Roads, cycling, and getting around
issues.description: How the city spends on streets: road repairs, sidewalks, bike lanes, e-mobility, and connections to the new SkyTrain stations.
issues.whatItAffects: Drivers, cyclists, pedestrians, transit riders, seniors, and businesses that rely on parking and deliveries.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the city's transportation budget and street design for city roads; TransLink and the province run transit and SkyTrain.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city prioritize on its streets?
viewQuestion.poleA: Expand bike lanes and other travel options alongside road upkeep
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus street budgets on road, sidewalk, and crosswalk repairs

tradeoffs.context: Street budgets are limited, so money for new travel options competes with money for repairing existing roads and sidewalks.

gains: More people may be able to bike, scoot, or walk safely to SkyTrain
Fewer car trips may ease congestion over time
costs: Less money may be left for road resurfacing
Some road space or parking may be reallocated

gains: Potholes, sidewalks, and crosswalks may be fixed sooner
Drivers may see smoother roads and fewer disruptions
costs: Fewer safe routes for people who bike or use e-mobility
Fewer travel choices as the city grows around SkyTrain

issues.title: Recreation and arts facilities
issues.description: Whether to keep planning an expanded Timms Community Centre with a performing arts centre and a year-round Al Anderson Pool.
issues.whatItAffects: Families, seniors, swimmers, arts groups, and taxpayers who would fund the projects.
issues.whoDecides: Council decides whether to continue planning and how to fund the projects; any borrowing would need a separate approval by electors.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city approach new facilities?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep planning the arts centre and year-round pool expansions
viewQuestion.poleB: Pause major facility projects and focus on maintaining what exists

tradeoffs.context: Major facilities can add long-term amenities, but they come with construction and operating costs that affect taxes.

gains: Year-round swimming and a local performing arts venue
More space for programs as the population grows
costs: Large capital and operating costs, possibly with borrowing
Other projects may compete for the same funds

gains: Lower long-term costs and less pressure on taxes
Budget can go to upkeep of existing facilities
costs: Residents may keep travelling elsewhere for year-round swimming and performances
Construction costs may be higher if projects are revived later

issues.title: Relationship with the Township and amalgamation
issues.description: Whether Langley City should stay a separate municipality or consider merging with the Township of Langley, amid disputes over shared services such as policing.
issues.whatItAffects: All City residents and businesses, City services and finances, and casino revenue the City now keeps.
issues.whoDecides: Council can negotiate service agreements and could ask residents for their view, but any amalgamation would require provincial approval and votes.

viewQuestion.question: What should the city's stance be on the Township?
viewQuestion.poleA: Keep Langley City a separate municipality
viewQuestion.poleB: Be open to merging with the Township if residents vote for it

tradeoffs.context: Staying separate keeps local control, while merging could change costs, services, and representation.

gains: Residents keep a council focused only on the City
The City keeps control of its own budget and revenues
costs: Disputes over shared services may continue
Some services may cost more to run separately

gains: Shared services and planning could be simpler across both Langleys
Residents get a direct say on the question
costs: City residents would be a small share of a larger municipality's voters
A merger process could take years and cost money to study

issues.title: Local economy and downtown
issues.description: How the city supports businesses, downtown Langley, and new jobs as SkyTrain arrives.
issues.whatItAffects: Business owners, workers, students, and people who shop and visit downtown.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets business licensing, permits, land use, business tax rates, and economic development programs such as the Innovation District plan.

viewQuestion.question: How should the city support local business?
viewQuestion.poleA: Use city plans and programs to attract new businesses and jobs
viewQuestion.poleB: Cut costs and red tape and let businesses lead growth

tradeoffs.context: City-led economic programs can attract investment but cost money, while lighter regulation leaves more to the market.

gains: New programs and hubs may draw entrepreneurs and employers
Planned districts can tie jobs to SkyTrain and Kwantlen
costs: Programs cost money and results can be uncertain
City priorities may not match what businesses want

gains: Lower costs and faster permits may help existing businesses
Less spending on programs may ease taxes
costs: Less coordinated planning for new job areas
Growth may depend more on outside market conditions

issues.title: Parks, trails, and trees
issues.description: How the city looks after its parks, trails, washrooms, and tree canopy as it grows.
issues.whatItAffects: Park and trail users, families, seniors, and nearby residents.
issues.whoDecides: Council sets the parks budget, maintenance levels, tree protection rules, and development requirements for green space.

viewQuestion.question: What should the parks budget focus on?
viewQuestion.poleA: Upgrade and expand parks, trails, and the tree canopy
viewQuestion.poleB: Focus on keeping existing parks clean, safe, and maintained

tradeoffs.context: Parks money is limited, so building new features competes with maintaining and securing what already exists.

gains: Wider, accessible trails and more shade and green space
More outdoor space for a growing population
costs: Higher capital and upkeep costs
Upgrades may compete with basic maintenance

gains: Existing parks and washrooms may be cleaner and feel safer
Lower long-term costs
costs: Fewer new trails, trees, and park features
Green space may not keep pace with growth

election.name: City of Langley general local election
election.howToVote: City of Langley voters can vote at Timms Community Centre (20399 Douglas Crescent) on General Voting Day, Saturday, Oct. 17, from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m., or at one of four advance voting days there. Voters already on the provincial voters list need no documents; others can register at the voting place with two pieces of ID that together show identity and residential address, at least one with a signature. Non-resident property electors had to register by Sept. 16.
election.voteByMail: Mail ballot applications had to be received by 4:30 p.m. Sept. 29 for mailed delivery; completed ballots must reach the City before 8 p.m. Oct. 17, by mail, the City Hall drop box, or in person.

ballotQuestions.question: Do you support Langley City continuing planning work on: expanding Timms Community Centre, combined with a new Performing Arts and Cultural Centre; and expanding Al Anderson Pool to provide year-round access?
ballotQuestions.summary: A non-binding Community Opinion Vote asking whether the next council should keep planning two facility expansions. It does not authorize construction or borrowing, which would need a separate approval process.

electorOrganizations.name: Achieving for Langley City
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes itself as an independent team that will listen to residents and make every tax dollar count, with priorities including safer streets, core services and responsible growth.

electorOrganizations.name: Langley City First
electorOrganizations.blurb: Describes itself as a team of long-time Langley City residents and independents focused on public safety, business growth and accountable local government.

notes: Ballot names are built as 'Surname, Given name' from the official Declaration of Candidates (Sept. 11, 2026); the PDF text extraction did not show exact legal/usual-name formatting, so verify against the PDF. Heather Jenkins appears in Langley Advance Times as Heather Creelman-Jenkins; the official list shows Heather Jenkins. Delaney Mack is a sitting councillor running for mayor (incumbent=false for the mayor race). Val van den Broek is a former mayor (2018-2022) and councillor, not a current incumbent. Incumbent councillors running: Albrecht, Solyom, Wallace. The declaration fetch summary once mentioned 17 councillor names but listed 16; the City page, localelections.ca and news all confirm 16. Langley City First's platform is published on the slate site and on Mayor Pachal's South Fraser Blog (sfb.nathanpachal.com, used as a candidate source). Slate council candidates with only general personal statements carry their slate's platform positions (sourceType affiliation_platform). Jennifer Denman and Samuel Otim have no website; only their official City profiles were found (general priorities, no issue stance). One Mack position (amalgamation) is from The Langley Union, a local online outlet, reporting her quote. CBC mayoral video (cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7335882) and a CBC article returned 403. No report of the Oct. 5 Chamber all-candidates forum was found yet. csdId 5915002 = Langley, City (CY), per StatCan 2021 Census Profile search result (5915001 is the Township). Ballot question is a non-binding Community Opinion Vote; wording as reported by Langley Advance Times (City page links to details).
